## ELI5

Keep a streamed download alive while its chunks are being saved, and clean it up after it becomes idle.

## What Changed

Refresh the existing cleanup timer only after a chunk has been written successfully. Reuse the native timer and retain the 30-minute cleanup interval, cancellation and renderer-lifetime cleanup.

## Why

The download session cleanup timer was armed once at start. Remote files and artifacts whose successful chunk writes continued longer than 30 minutes were deleted mid-transfer, even though the session was active.

Production callers:

- src/renderer/src/runtime/files/reads/runtime-remote-file-download.ts:streamDownloadedFile sequentially reads 512 KiB chunks and calls fs:appendDownloadedFileChunk
- src/main/ipc/filesystem/downloads/filesystem-download-handlers.ts:startDownloadedFile and appendDownloadedFileChunk

## Linked Issue

Fixes #50623

## Visual Proof

N/A — this change affects backend processing and has no graphical layout change. The production behavior is reproduced below.

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| The timer was measured from session creation, so at the scaled equivalent of 40 minutes the active session and its staging bytes had already been deleted. | Successful progress keeps the session and exact bytes available. The later idle interval removes them. A failed write does not extend the session lifetime. |

## Testing

- [x] I manually tested the source-level production reproduction described here
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below
- [x] No permanent tests added; the policy reason and baseline-failing manual reproduction are provided

No permanent IPC wiring or elapsed-time test was added, following the repository test policy. The linked issue contains the complete standalone probe. The original source fails the active-session assertion; the changed source passes active-progress, idle-cleanup and failed-write cases. Native timers and real file writes are used; only the long timeout is scaled and the Electron dialog/IPC boundary is supplied locally.

Use the standalone reproduction in the linked issue. From the source checkout:

```sh
ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1 node --import tsx /absolute/path/to/repro.mjs .
```

Locally exercised on Linux with Node 24.22.3. No macOS, Windows, graphical desktop, physical remote host or live external provider execution is claimed.

Final integrated validation: 32 focused regression tests in 22 files passed, including the unchanged archive-write failure case that had timed out under earlier heavy concurrent checking. The Drive performance contract passed separately (1 file/1 test). Changed-code quality passed with zero new findings across 129 changed paths; final touched-file formatting and git diff --check passed. Node typechecking passed for 17,026 files and web typechecking for 16,094 files using the repository-supported Bun compiler with one worker. These are aggregate validation results for the prepared contributions, not per-PR test counts.

The required `pnpm check:changed --base=9890ea181c0f9ae59fb82da64c4a6fbc0504a817` was attempted after the final edits. Its workspace-package build is blocked because this environment rejects the tsx CLI local IPC socket (`listen EPERM`). The default tsrs typechecker was also terminated with SIGKILL; the supported Bun typechecking route completed successfully. The complete gate/build is not claimed to pass and still requires CI.

## Performance

One native Timeout.refresh call per successfully written chunk, reusing the existing timer. The renderer streams sequential 512 KiB chunks, so this adds no timer allocation, background polling or extra file operation.

## Risk

**Level:** Low

Active sessions can now last longer than 30 minutes in total, which is the intended behavior. Abandoned sessions still expire after 30 idle minutes. Failed writes do not refresh the timer; cancellation and renderer destruction still close the session. The elapsed-time probe used a scaled native timeout, not a 40-minute wall-clock run.

A plain revert restores the previous behavior; no schema migration is introduced.

## AI Disclosure

Core contribution owner: @Afloat16. Required tooling disclosure: GPT-6 Astra Pro was used for implementation and review.

## Review

Reviewed the production caller, the original failure, ordinary controls, error cleanup and concurrency boundaries. Platform and persistence risks are described above. Existing public interfaces and remote protocol formats are retained.

## Notes

The user's prior contribution history and targeted repository PR/issue searches were checked for an equivalent change. Related work reviewed for distinct scope:

- #23108 handles renderer lifetime and late file opens; its full body does not refresh the timer for active writes.
- #35636/#7738/#6436 originate or use the download handlers; no active-session idle-expiry fix.

## ELI5

When you read a Google Doc with `orca docs read`, Orca only looked at the first 100 comments. Resolved comments count toward those 100, so a doc with lots of old resolved feedback could show "no open comments" even though open ones were sitting further down. Orca now keeps reading the comment list until it has them all, up to a sensible limit. If it has to stop early, it says the count is "at least N".

## What Changed

- **Before:** `openComments` (`src/main/google/google-docs-comments.ts`) made one Drive `comments.list` call with `pageSize=100`. The `fields` mask left out `nextPageToken`, so Drive never sent back a continuation token, and there was no loop. If the first 100 comments were all resolved, the read said `[Orca: no open comments]` and `openComments` was 0.
- **After:**
  - The `fields` mask asks for `nextPageToken`, and `openComments` follows pages, filtering and clipping each page as before. It stops after `MAX_COMMENT_PAGES = 20` pages (2,000 comments). This uses the same bounded `for` loop as the Gmail and Calendar change readers, so a Drive token that repeats can't spin forever.
  - `openComments` now returns `{ comments, more }`. `more` is true when pages were left unread, either because the cap was hit or because a request for page 2 or later failed. A failure on page 1 still fails the read, as it does on main. A failure on a later page keeps what was already read, so one bad comment page no longer loses the doc text too.
  - `readDoc` sets the new optional `DocsReadView.moreComments` when `more` is true. `formatDocsRead` then prints `[Orca: N+ open comments]` and `[Orca: N+ more not shown; they are in the doc]`, so a partial count is never shown as exact.
  - Later pages of a doc (`--offset > 0`) show no comment lines, so they still read just one comment page, as on main. The `--json` `openComments` field is still there, and `moreComments` marks it as a lower bound.

## Why

Without the continuation token, docs with long comment histories silently lost open feedback, and agents reading the doc never saw it. The page cap keeps an explicit read bounded in time, and the `+` marker means a capped or partial count is never presented as exact. We chose that over reading without a cap, which risked unbounded loops and CLI timeouts on huge docs. We also chose it over failing the whole read when a later page fails, which would throw away the doc text over one comment page.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #50519

## Visual Proof

N/A. No UI change. This only affects the text of the `orca docs read` CLI/RPC. Here is the data-level before and after for a doc whose first comment page is all resolved and whose open comment is on page 3:

| Before (main) | After |
| --- | --- |
| `[Orca: no open comments]`, `openComments: 0` | `[Orca: 1 open comment]` with the comment shown, `openComments: 1` |
| Doc with more than 2,000 comments: count silently too low | `[Orca: N+ open comments]`, `moreComments: true` |

## Testing

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below
- [x] Every added test fails without this change and avoids the [test anti-patterns](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/blob/main/docs/agents-md-refs/test-antipatterns.md)

- `src/main/google/google-docs-comments.test.ts` uses a type-checked fake `GoogleApi` that, like Drive, only returns fields named in the `fields` mask. It covers four cases:
  - Open comments past a resolved page and an empty page. This fails on main (`[]`).
  - The 20-page cap when Drive repeats a token. Without the cap the loop never ends.
  - Keeping collected comments when a later page fails.
  - A later doc page (`--offset`) making exactly one comments call and reporting `moreComments`.
- `src/cli/google/google-files-format.test.ts` covers the `1+` (plural), `2+ more not shown`, and `0+` wording.
- `vitest` on both files: 5 pass. Clean on all 6 touched files: oxlint, oxfmt, the anti-slop gate, native code-quality oxlint, ast-grep, and the changed-code quality gate.
- Tested on macOS (unit level, no live Google account). The change is platform-independent.

## Performance

None on any hot path. This only runs on an explicit `orca docs read` (an on-demand async RPC in the main process), not during startup, polling or rendering. A doc with 100 comments or fewer still makes exactly one request. Larger docs make one extra network round trip per 100 comments, at most 20, and only when Drive returns a token. Later doc pages still make one request. In a microbenchmark with 100 comments per page, CPU per page was about 0.2-0.5 ms, and 20 pages took about 0.5 ms in total, so nothing stalls past 16 ms. There is no new sync I/O, subprocess work or polling. Comment output stays within the existing 3,000-character budget.

## Risk

**Level:** Low

The riskiest part is that first-page reads of very large docs take longer, up to 20 sequential Drive calls. `moreComments` is optional, so older CLIs and paired clients just ignore it and keep showing the number. A plain revert backs this out. There is no stored data or schema migration.

## Review

Original fix by @Afloat16 in #50520 (Afloat is credited as co-author on the commit). The maintainer changes are the page cap, the lower-bound `moreComments` flag and formatter wording, the single-page read for `--offset`, keeping partial results when a later page fails, and replacing the credential-file test fixture with a focused fake.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Notes

Ensure no issues in: Security, Cross-platform support (Linux, Windows, Mac), Remote SSH, Mobile, general backwards compatibility, performance

No new endpoints or commands. It uses the same Drive `comments.list` endpoint with `pageToken`. Mixed versions are safe because the new field is optional.

## Checklist

- [x] I explained what changed and why (ELI5, the user-facing before/after, the mechanism, and why over the alternatives)
- [x] I stated the risk: what could break, for whom, and how to back it out

- [x] Cross-platform, SSH/remote, and path/shortcut impact considered (or N/A)
- [ ] `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, and `pnpm build` pass (or CI will cover; local preferred)

## ELI5

Google hands back your calendar list in pages of 250. Orca only read the first page, so if you had more calendars than that, it couldn't find the ones further down by name. Worse, if two calendars shared a name and one was on a later page, Orca just took the first one instead of asking you which you meant. Now Orca reads every page.

## What Changed

- **Before:** `listCalendarEntries` in `src/main/google/google-calendar-read.ts` fetched one `calendarList` page (`maxResults=250`) and ignored `nextPageToken`. On accounts with more than 250 calendars:
  - `pickCalendar` threw `No calendar is named "..."` for a calendar on page 2 or later, and `orca calendar list --calendars` left those calendars out.
  - A name on page 1 that appeared again on a later page was not reported as ambiguous. The page-1 calendar was returned, so event writes (`google-calendar-write.ts`, `google-calendar-event-target.ts`) could land on the wrong calendar.
- **After:** `CalendarListSchema` now parses `nextPageToken`, and `listCalendarEntries` follows it and collects entries from every page. Paging stops after 20 pages (5,000 calendars) so a misbehaving token can't loop forever. Lookups by ID or `primary` are unchanged.

## Why

Google's `calendarList.list` returns `nextPageToken` until the last page. Following it is the only way to get the full list. The loop works the same way as the existing paging in `google-calendar-changes.ts` and `google-gmail-changes.ts`.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #50511

## Visual Proof

N/A. This changes CLI/RPC data results, not the UI. Before/after on the same two-page fixture:

| | Before (main) | After (this PR) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pickCalendar(api, 'boardroom')`, calendar on page 2 | `GoogleToolError: No calendar is named "boardroom"` | resolves `room@example.com` |
| `pickCalendar(api, 'Planning')`, on page 1 and page 2 | silently returns the page-1 calendar | `Several calendars are named "Planning"; pass one's id: one@example.com, two@example.com.` |

## Testing

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below
- [x] Every added test fails without this change and avoids the [test anti-patterns](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/blob/main/docs/agents-md-refs/test-antipatterns.md)

- New `src/main/google/google-calendar-list-pagination.test.ts` calls the real `pickCalendar` with a stubbed HTTP layer that returns two pages. It checks that a name on a later page resolves (case-insensitively) and that a duplicate across pages is refused, using the full error message. It fails on main and passes on this branch.
- Extra probe cases, kept out of the PR: empty middle pages, page tokens that need URL escaping, `maxResults` kept on every request, `listCalendars` returning every page, and an unknown name still failing after all pages are read. All fail on main and pass here.
- All `src/main/google` tests pass (7 files, 54 tests). The touched files pass oxlint, oxfmt, anti-slop, native code-quality plugins, ast-grep and the changed-code quality gate.
- Tested on macOS (unit level). The code is platform-neutral async network I/O.

## Performance

None on any hot path. This only runs when a user runs a calendar command (`orca calendar list/get/create/update` or free-time) and is not polled. The trigger checker uses `google-calendar-changes.ts` and doesn't call this code. There is no new sync I/O and no new subprocess. Benchmark with stubbed HTTP, 250 entries per page:
- Typical (1 page): about 0.3 ms average either way, 1 request. No change.
- Adversarial: at 20 pages (5,000 calendars) the average is about 5 ms with 20 requests. At 25 pages, the cap holds it to 20 requests (about 4.8 ms average) instead of 25 uncapped (about 10.7 ms average). Main took 1 request but gave the wrong answer. The extra time is the network round-trips needed for a correct result. All awaits are async, so nothing stalls the main process.

## Risk

**Level:** Low

The riskiest part is the extra requests for users with more than 250 calendars. Each request already has the existing per-request timeout. A name that used to resolve silently to the wrong calendar now returns an "ambiguous" error that asks for the calendar ID. Calendars past 5,000 are still not read, which is far beyond realistic accounts. To back it out, revert the commit. There is no schema or saved-data change.
